title: Sati's mistake
hookLine: a monk says the same consciousness wanders on unchanged; the Buddha: consciousness arises from conditions

lines: A LITTLE SOMEONE BEHIND THE EYES.
cards: Most of us carry a quiet picture of ourselves: somewhere behind the eyes, a little someone who watches, listens and remembers, the same one at five and at fifty.
A monk named Sati, a fisherman's son, carried that picture too, and he was sure the Buddha taught it.

As I understand the teaching, he told the other monks, it's this same consciousness that runs on and wanders through birth after birth, not another one. The other monks tried to talk him out of it. He wouldn't budge.

teach.h: SATI: THE SAME CONSCIOUSNESS GOES ON
teach.b: So the monks bring him to the Buddha, in the greater discourse on the ending of craving, the thirty-eighth of the Middle-Length Sayings. Is it true you hold this view? It is, Sati says.
What is this consciousness, then? It's what speaks and feels, he answers, and experiences the results of good and bad deeds here and there. The Buddha's reply is blunt.
He calls Sati a misguided man: to whom have you ever heard me teach it that way?
Haven't I said many times that consciousness arises from conditions, and without a condition, there's no consciousness at all? Then a picture.

teach.h: A FIRE IS NAMED BY ITS FUEL
teach.b: A fire is named by what it burns. Burning logs, it's a log fire. Burning grass, a grass fire.
Burning dung, a dung fire. There's no fire apart from its fuel. Consciousness is named the same way.
Arising because of the eye and a sight, it's eye-consciousness. Because of the ear and a sound, ear-consciousness. Because of the mind and a thought, mind-consciousness.
No little someone sits behind the eyes, waiting, unchanged. Each moment of knowing is lit by what it's knowing.

Buddhist schools later worked this out in different ways, including how continuity carries from life to life, but they keep the Buddha's point: consciousness isn't a thing that travels. It's a process that arises.
Sati's mistake is easy to make; it's the picture most of us start with. The Buddha didn't replace it with nothing. He replaced it with fire.

how: Buddhist teachers use MN 38's fire simile to explain that consciousness arises dependent on conditions; in meditation many practitioners watch seeing, hearing and thinking arise and pass with their objects.

o: breaking a monastery rule without knowing
taking the mind for one unchanging traveler
forgetting to stay mindful while sitting

games.q: fire and its fuel — tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha agreed that one consciousness wanders unchanged from life to life
he rebuked Sati: he had always taught that consciousness arises from conditions.
in the simile, a fire is named by what it burns
log fire, grass fire, dung fire; consciousness is named by eye, ear, mind and their objects.
the text names him Sati, son of a fisherman.

games.q: you're one of the monks. Sati keeps insisting the Buddha taught that the same consciousness wanders on. you've tried to talk him out of it. what do you do next?
o: let him teach it; maybe he's right.
games.why: the monks bring the matter to the Buddha, who asks Sati directly and then teaches the fire simile to the whole community.

practice: Close your eyes and wait for a sound, a car, a fan, a bird, your own breath, and notice that hearing doesn't come before the sound: it lights up with it, like fire catching on dry grass.
When the sound fades, hearing that sound fades too, and you wait for the next small fire.

wordCard.voice: Sati's mistake. Taking consciousness for one unchanging traveler, when the Buddha taught it arises from conditions, like fire from its fuel.

orig.note: Pali vinnana: consciousness, the knowing that arises with eye, ear, nose, tongue, body or mind.

carryVoice: Your line: from conditions. A fire named by its fuel, not a traveler. Day four hundred thirty-three, complete.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 38, Mahatanhasankhaya Sutta (the greater discourse on the destruction of craving), opening section
